claims.source: Intriguingly, many transcripts with the greatest medial (97) or lateral (56) enrichment (e.g. >1.5X in medial vs. lateral tissue or vice versa) in the intestine were expressed by goblet cells (Figure 2C–F, Supplementary file 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2C–F, Supplementary file 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data.

claims.claim: GO analysis of the most medially and laterally enriched transcripts suggested possible functional specialization of goblet cells with respect to lipid metabolism, protein processing, extracellular matrix organization, and innate immunity.
claims.source: GO analysis of these transcripts suggested possible functional specialization with respect to lipid metabolism, protein processing, extracellular matrix organization, and innate immunity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E and Figure 6—source data 1I–J).
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on GO analysis and references Figure 6—figure supplement 2E as supporting data.

claims.claim: Goblet cells express pancreatic carboxypeptidase A2 and lipase F/gastric triacylglycerol lipase, which are predicted to be secreted regulators of protein and triglyceride catabolism.
claims.source: For example, in support of previous suggestions that goblet cells promote luminal digestion (Arnold, 1909; Pedersen, 1961; Jennings, 1962), we identified several goblet-enriched transcripts predicted to encode secreted regulators of protein catabolism (pancreatic carboxypeptidase A2) and triglyceride catabolism (lipase F/gastric triacylglycerol lipase) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Three goblet-enriched kallikreins were identified.
claims.source: Second, we also identified three goblet-enriched kallikreins (klk) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), secreted proteases whose mammalian homologs produce vasoactive plasma kinin, but also hydrolyze extracellular matrix molecules, growth factors, hormone proteins, and antimicrobial peptides in numerous tissues (Prassas et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Kallikreins are expressed by goblet cells in rat, cat, and mouse intestines.
claims.source: Kallikreins are expressed by goblet cells in rat, cat, and mouse intestines (Schachter et al., 1986; Grün et al., 2016), and have been implicated in inflammatory bowel disease and gastrointestinal cancers (Stadnicki, 2011; Kontos et al., 2013), suggesting additional conservation of planarian goblet cell physiology.
claims.evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Goblet cells express peptidoglycan recognition protein (pgrp-1b).
claims.source: Third, goblet cells express peptidoglycan recognition protein (pgrp-1b) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), whose vertebrate and invertebrate homologs modulate innate immune signaling and play direct bactericidal roles (Kurata, 2014; Dziarski and Gupta, 2018), suggesting goblet cells may coordinate immune responses and/or regulate microbiome composition.
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: A homolog of prohormone convertase (pcsk1) is enriched in goblet cells and peripharyngeal cells.
claims.source: Fourth, a homolog of prohormone convertase (pcsk1) is enriched in goblet cells, as well as peripharyngeal cells surrounding the pharynx (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3C as supporting data.

claims.claim: Prohormone convertases (PCs) cleave neuropeptide and peptide hormone preproteins to generate bioactive peptides.
claims.source: Prohormone convertases (PCs) cleave neuropeptide and peptide hormone preproteins to generate bioactive peptides.
claims.evidence: The text states this as established knowledge.

claims.claim: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, PCs function in neurons and in endocrine cell types such as pancreatic islet cells and digestive tract enteroendocrine cells, where they regulate glucose levels, energy homeostasis, and appetite.
claims.source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, PCs function in neurons, but also in endocrine cell types such as pancreatic islet cells and digestive tract enteroendocrine cells, where they regulate glucose levels, energy homeostasis, and appetite (Grün et al., 2016; Pauls et al., 2014; Stijnen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: pcsk1 expression suggests goblet cells may play an enteroendocrine-like role.
claims.source: Although another planarian pcsk paralog, Smed-pc2, processes neuropeptides required for germline development (Collins et al., 2010), to our knowledge, no intestine-enriched prohormones have been reported. Nonetheless, pcsk1 expression suggests goblet cells may play an enteroendocrine-like role, as in other organisms.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on pcsk1 expression and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Genes encoding planarian homologs of gel-forming mucins were expressed by peripharyngeal cells that send projections into the pharynx, not by goblet cells.
claims.source: Finally, we were surprised to find that genes encoding planarian homologs of gel-forming mucins (which we identified in separate bioinformatic searches) were expressed not by goblet cells, but by peripharyngeal cells that send projections into the pharynx (Forsthoefel et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3D as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Some planarian gel-forming mucin proteins may be delivered to the intestinal lumen through the pharynx.
claims.source: While additional goblet-enriched proteins with mucin-like roles might exist (Bocchinfuso et al., 2012; Syed et al., 2008), these expression patterns suggest that some planarian gel-forming mucin proteins are delivered to the intestinal lumen through the pharynx, and indicate a possible difference between planarian and vertebrate intestinal goblet cells (Birchenough et al., 2015; Chang et al., 1994; Johansson et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on expression patterns and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: The intestine expresses numerous homologs of transcripts that are enriched in human GI tissues.
claims.source: Further illustrating the conservation of physiological roles, we found that the intestine expresses numerous homologs of transcripts that are enriched in human GI tissues (Figure 7A–E, Supplementary file 4, and Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7A–E, Supplementary file 4, and Figure 7—source data 1 as supporting data.

claims.claim: 5583 planarian transcripts encoding predicted ORFs have high homology to ORFs in UniProt human transcripts.
claims.source: To make this comparison, we conducted reciprocal best homology (RBH) searches (Bork et al., 1998; Tatusov et al., 1997) to identify 5583 planarian transcripts encoding predicted open reading frames (ORFs) with high homology to ORFs in UniProt human transcripts (The UniProt Consortium, 2018), and vice versa (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7A–B as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Four of the five tissues to which the planarian intestine was most similar are involved in digestion or energy storage/metabolism.
claims.source: Strikingly, four of the five tissues to which the planarian intestine was most similar are involved in digestion (duodenum, small intestine, and gallbladder) or energy storage/metabolism (liver) (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7E as supporting data.

claims.claim: The planarian intestine was also similar to other human digestive tissues (esophagus, colon, and rectum), as well as kidney.
claims.source: The intestine was also similar to other human digestive tissues (esophagus, colon, and rectum), as well as kidney, possibly suggesting a role supporting the planarian protonephridial system in filtration or processing of extracellular solutes (Figure 7E; Thi-Kim Vu et al., 2015; Rink et al., 2011; Scimone et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7E as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Duodenum- and small intestine-enriched RBH transcripts included predicted regulators of endodermal specification, bile transport, lipid metabolism, and glucose transport.
claims.source: Duodenum- and small intestine-enriched RBH transcripts included predicted regulators of endodermal specification, bile transport, lipid metabolism, and glucose transport (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding.

claims.claim: RBH homologs enriched in liver included several predicted regulators of glucose, amino acid, lipid, and xenobiotic compound metabolism.
claims.source: In addition, RBH homologs enriched in liver included several predicted regulators of glucose, amino acid, lipid, and xenobiotic compound metabolism (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding.

claims.claim: Physiological roles performed by multiple human digestive organs are consolidated in the planarian intestine.
claims.source: These observations reinforce the evolutionary conservation of intestinal gene expression and indicate that physiological roles performed by multiple human digestive organs are consolidated in the planarian intestine.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claims.claim: Knockdown of gli-1 dramatically reduced goblet cells at the midline in regenerating intestine in tail fragments.
claims.source: Knockdown of a second transcription factor, gli-1 (a transducer of hedgehog signaling [Rink et al., 2009; Glazer et al., 2010]), caused failure of goblet cells to regenerate at the midline of the new anterior branch in amputated tail fragments regenerating a new head (Figure 8A–B, Supplementary file 5C, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B, Supplementary file 5C, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: In gli-1(RNAi) animals, goblet cells were less abundant in pre-existing regions of the intestine, particularly in lateral intestinal branches.
claims.source: In addition, goblet cells were less abundant in pre-existing regions of the intestine, particularly in lateral intestinal branches (Figure 8A–B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claims.claim: Regeneration of goblet cells was reduced in new tail branches of gli-1(RNAi) head fragments and in anterior and posterior branches in gli-1(RNAi) trunk fragments.
claims.source: Regeneration of goblet cells was also reduced in new tail branches of gli-1(RNAi) head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) and in anterior and posterior branches in gli-1(RNAi) trunk fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 2B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2C as supporting data.

claims.claim: Effects of gli-1 knockdown on goblet cells were specific, since phagocytes and basal cells regenerated normally.
claims.source: These effects on goblet cells were specific, since phagocytes (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C) and basal cells (Figure 8B) regenerated normally.
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A, Figure 8B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claims.claim: In RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cells appeared to differentiate normally in regenerating intestine, including at the midline of anterior intestinal branches in tail fragments.
claims.source: By contrast to the gli-1 phenotype, goblet cells appeared to differentiate normally in regenerating intestine upon knockdown of a third TF, ras-responsive element binding protein 2 (RREB2), including at the midline of anterior intestinal branches in tail fragments (Figure 8A–B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A), in posterior branches in head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), and in both anterior and posterior branches in trunk fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claims.claim: In RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, new goblet cells were largely restricted to the midline/primary branches in tail and trunk regenerates.
claims.source: However, in tail and trunk regenerates, new goblet cells were largely restricted to the midline/primary branches (Figure 8A–B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and C), and were less abundant in posterior branches of head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claims.claim: In RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cell numbers were dramatically reduced or completely absent in pre-existing intestinal regions, especially lateral branches.
claims.source: Furthermore, in pre-existing intestinal regions (especially lateral branches), goblet cell numbers were dramatically reduced or even completely absent. These included the posterior of tail fragments (Figure 8A–B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A), the anterior of head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), and central regions of trunk fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claims.claim: In RREB2(RNAi) animals, phagocytes and basal cells were unaffected.
claims.source: As with gli-1, phagocytes and basal cells were unaffected (Figure 8A–B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claims.claim: gli-1 regulates neoblast fate specification and/or differentiation of neoblast progeny into goblet cells in new intestinal branches.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that gli-1 regulates neoblast fate specification and/or differentiation of neoblast progeny into goblet cells in new intestinal branches, while RREB2 may control maintenance or survival of goblet cells after they initially differentiate.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claims.claim: RREB2 may control maintenance or survival of goblet cells after they initially differentiate.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that gli-1 regulates neoblast fate specification and/or differentiation of neoblast progeny into goblet cells in new intestinal branches, while RREB2 may control maintenance or survival of goblet cells after they initially differentiate.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claims.claim: In uninjured animals, gli-1 knockdown reduced goblet cell numbers, especially in anterior, posterior, and lateral intestine branches.
claims.source: Knockdown of gli-1 reduced goblet cell numbers in uninjured animals, especially in anterior, posterior, and lateral intestine branches (Figure 8C), but many goblet cells remained in medial, primary intestinal branches.
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8C as supporting data.

claims.claim: In RREB2(RNAi) uninjured animals, goblet cells were more dramatically reduced in all regions of the intestine.
claims.source: In RREB2(RNAi) animals, goblet cells were more dramatically reduced in all regions of the intestine (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8C as supporting data.

claims.claim: In gli-1(RNAi) uninjured animals, almost no lateral goblet cells remained, while medial goblet cells were much less affected.
claims.source: Indeed, we found (using additional goblet cell markers) that almost no lateral goblet cells remained in gli-1(RNAi) uninjured animals, while again, medial goblet cells were much less affected (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3A as supporting data.

claims.claim: In RREB2(RNAi) uninjured animals, reduction of both medial and lateral goblet cell numbers was pronounced, but some lateral goblet cells remained.
claims.source: By contrast, in RREB2(RNAi) uninjured animals, reduction of both medial and lateral goblet cell numbers was pronounced, but nonetheless some lateral goblet cells remained (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3A as supporting data.

claims.claim: In gli-1(RNAi) tail regenerates, both medial and lateral goblet cell subpopulations failed to differentiate in the primary anterior intestinal branch.
claims.source: For example, both subpopulations failed to differentiate in the primary anterior intestinal branch in gli-1(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B), and both subpopulations were severely reduced in pre-existing, posterior branches of RREB2(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3B as supporting data.

claims.claim: In RREB2(RNAi) tail regenerates, both medial and lateral goblet cell subpopulations were severely reduced in pre-existing, posterior branches.
claims.source: For example, both subpopulations failed to differentiate in the primary anterior intestinal branch in gli-1(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B), and both subpopulations were severely reduced in pre-existing, posterior branches of RREB2(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3B as supporting data.

claims.claim: In uninjured animals undergoing normal homeostatic growth and renewal, gli-1 is primarily required for differentiation of new lateral intestinal cells.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that, in uninjured animals undergoing normal homeostatic growth and renewal, gli-1 is primarily required for differentiation of new lateral intestinal cells.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claims.claim: RREB2 is required for maintenance of both medial and lateral goblet cells, although lateral cell numbers are slightly less affected by RREB2 knockdown compared to gli-1.
claims.source: Conversely, RREB2 seems to be required for maintenance of both medial and lateral goblet cells, although lateral cell numbers are slightly less affected by RREB2 knockdown, compared to gli-1.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claims.claim: Mechanisms regulating goblet cell differentiation and maintenance may differ during homeostasis and regeneration.
claims.source: These complex observations suggest that mechanisms regulating goblet cell differentiation and maintenance may differ during homeostasis and regeneration, or that compensatory mechanisms capable of sustaining goblet cell production/survival in uninjured gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals are insufficient to meet the increased demand for new tissue during regeneration.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claims.claim: gli-1 mRNA is most highly enriched in phagocytes, basal cells, and intestine-associated muscle cells (visceral muscle), but is also expressed at lower levels in some goblet cells.
claims.source: In fact, gli-1, which was previously shown to be expressed by intestine-associated cells (Rink et al., 2009; Currie et al., 2016), was most highly enriched in phagocytes, basal cells, and intestine-associated muscle cells (visceral muscle), but was also expressed at lower levels in some goblet cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 4A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: RREB2 mRNA is enriched in goblet cells and basal cells, but expression was also observed in some phagocytes and intestine-associated muscle.
claims.source: RREB2 was enriched in goblet cells and basal cells, but expression was also observed in some phagocytes and intestine-associated muscle (Figure 8—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 4B as supporting data.

claims.claim: Knockdown of fer1 (PTF1A) and lhx2b modestly reduced goblet cells in pre-existing branches.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we found that knockdown of two other TFs, 48 related 1 (fer1) (also called pancreas transcription factor one subunit alpha or PTF1A [Fincher et al., 2018]), and LIM homeobox 2 (lhx2b), also modestly reduced goblet cells in pre-existing branches (Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–C and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–C and Supplementary file 5 as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: mRNAs encoding fer1 (PTF1A) and lhx2b are enriched in basal regions of the intestine.
claims.source: mRNAs encoding these TFs are enriched in basal regions of the intestine (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1 as supporting data.

claims.claim: Single-cell transcriptome data suggest PTF1A expression is elevated in differentiating neoblast progeny in the basal cell lineage.
claims.source: In addition, single-cell transcriptome data suggest PTF1A expression is elevated in differentiating neoblast progeny in the basal cell lineage (Fincher et al., 2018), and PTF1A also reduces basal intestinal cell numbers (Fincher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: PTF1A reduces basal intestinal cell numbers.
claims.source: In addition, single-cell transcriptome data suggest PTF1A expression is elevated in differentiating neoblast progeny in the basal cell lineage (Fincher et al., 2018), and PTF1A also reduces basal intestinal cell numbers (Fincher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claims.claim: Basal cells (and possibly phagocytes or muscle cells) may non-autonomously influence goblet cell differentiation and/or survival.
claims.source: Thus, although our data support a role for gli-1 and RREB2 in goblet cells and/or their precursors, they also raise the possibility that basal cells (and possibly phagocytes or muscle cells) may non-autonomously influence goblet cell differentiation and/or survival.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claims.claim: Some uninjured gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) planarians refused food and failed to eat after 4–5 weeks of dsRNA feeding.
claims.source: Over a 6 week dsRNA feeding regimen, some uninjured gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) planarians refused food and failed to eat after 4–5 weeks (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8D as supporting data.

claims.claim: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals, some animals eventually lysed, curled, or died.
claims.source: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals, some animals eventually lysed, curled, or died (Figure 8—figure supplement 6A), suggesting that goblet cells are required for viability.
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 6A as supporting data.

claims.claim: Goblet cells are required for viability.
claims.source: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals, some animals eventually lysed, curled, or died (Figure 8—figure supplement 6A), suggesting that goblet cells are required for viability.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented and references Figure 8—figure supplement 6A as supporting data.

claims.claim: A modest (but insignificant) decrease in animal size was observed in RREB2(RNAi) planarians relative to controls.
claims.source: Additionally, we observed a modest (but insignificant) decrease in animal size (Figure 8—figure supplement 6B–C) in RREB2(RNAi) planarians relative to controls.
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 6B–C as supporting data.

claims.claim: Feeding failure and other phenotypes were only observed in animals fed dsRNA 1x/week for 6 weeks, not in animals fed 2x/week for six times.
claims.source: Interestingly, we only observed feeding failure and other phenotypes in animals fed the dsRNA/liver mix 1x/week (every 7 days) for 6 weeks; animals that were fed 2x/week (every 3–4 days), but still six times, did not refuse to eat, lyse, curl, or die (not shown).
claims.evidence: The text states this observation.

claims.claim: Goblet cells may regulate hunger (or other aspects of digestive physiology) primarily in starved animals.
claims.source: This suggests that goblet cells may regulate hunger (or other aspects of digestive physiology) primarily in starved animals, consistent with expression of prohormone convertase (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C), above.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3C as supporting data.

claims.claim: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cell depletion was robust, but neither gene was required more generally for regeneration.
claims.source: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cell depletion was robust (Figure 8A–B), but neither gene was required more generally for regeneration (with the infrequent exception of reduced posterior blastemas in gli-1(RNAi) regenerates, mentioned above), as the brain (Figure 8E), pharynx (Figure 8E), other intestinal cell types (Figure 8A–B), and new intestinal branches (Figure 8A–B) all regenerated without noticeable defects.
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8E as supporting data.

claims.claim: Goblet cells are broadly dispensable for regeneration.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that goblet cells are broadly dispensable for regeneration, and that their primary role may be to regulate appetite or other aspects of intestinal physiology that contribute to viability.
claims.evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

results.result: The authors developed and optimized a laser-capture microdissection (LCM) protocol for planarian intestinal tissue that preserves RNA integrity suitable for RNA-Seq. Methacarn fixation, magnesium relaxation, and rapid Eosin Y staining were identified as optimal conditions, enabling extraction of high-quality RNA from microdissected medial intestine, lateral intestine, and non-intestine tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C29, C30, and C33-C36 describe methodological optimization and validation. The text explicitly states that prominent 18S/28S rRNA peaks indicated RNA of sufficient quality for RNA-Seq (C36), and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 provides supporting data for fixation and staining comparisons (C33-C35). The methods are clearly described and validated.

results.result: RNA-Seq of laser-captured intestinal tissue identified 1,844 intestine-enriched transcripts, including 1,748 upregulated in medial intestine and 1,627 in lateral intestine. Validation by WISH confirmed 88% (143/162) of tested transcripts had detectable intestinal expression, including transcripts with medial, lateral, or uniform expression patterns, as well as anteriorly and posteriorly enriched transcripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 present RNA-Seq results with specific numerical data and validation rates. The high WISH validation rate (88%, C42) and concordance between RNA-Seq predictions and in situ expression patterns (C43-C44) strongly support the transcriptome characterization. Figure 1 provides supporting data for transcript counts and expression patterns.

results.result: Spatial LCM and FISH revealed previously unappreciated regionalization of intestinal cell types along the medio-lateral axis, particularly among goblet cells. Distinct medial and lateral goblet cell subpopulations were identified that rarely co-mingled or co-expressed markers at boundaries. Subpopulations of basal cells in lateral regions and transcripts expressed by multiple cell types in different combinations were also discovered.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C31, and C60-C64 describe spatial heterogeneity validated by FISH. Figure 4 provides clear visual evidence of distinct medial and lateral goblet cell populations with minimal overlap (C62). The discovery of cell-type diversity is well-supported by both RNA-Seq data and microscopy.

results.result: Comparison of LCM transcriptomes with sorted phagocyte data distinguished transcripts expressed by three intestinal cell types: phagocytes (900 transcripts upregulated in both datasets), goblet cells, and basal cells. WISH validation identified 91 transcripts with ubiquitous/phagocyte-like expression, 25 goblet-cell-enriched transcripts, and 25 basal-cell-enriched transcripts, with some goblet-cell transcripts showing medial or lateral enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C55 integrate LCM and sorted phagocyte data to classify cell-type-specific expression. The approach is logical and well-validated by WISH (C54-C55). Figure 2 provides supporting scatter plots and expression patterns. The identification of three distinct cell types is convincingly demonstrated.

results.result: FISH confirmed that phagocytes (ctsla+), goblet cells (npc2+), and basal cells (slc22a6+) are three distinct intestinal cell types with minimal marker overlap. Basal cells occupy basal regions around digestive cells and are distinct from visceral muscle fibers, representing a novel cell type independently confirmed by single-cell sequencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 describe FISH validation of cell-type identity. Figure 3 provides clear confocal images showing distinct expression patterns with minimal overlap. The conclusion that basal cells are a novel cell type (C59) is supported by both the authors' data and citation of independent single-cell sequencing (Fincher et al., 2018).

results.result: Comparison with single-cell RNA-Seq studies showed considerable agreement in cell-type enrichment predictions, but LCM identified 809 additional intestine-enriched transcripts not detected by scRNA-Seq, with 22/28 validated by WISH. The authors suggest LCM may be more sensitive than current single-cell approaches for detecting tissue-specific gene expression when single-cell resolution is not required.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C72 compare LCM and scRNA-Seq approaches. The high validation rate (79%, C69) for LCM-exclusive transcripts supports the claim of superior sensitivity (C72). However, the inference about sensitivity (C72) is somewhat speculative, as incomplete overlap could also reflect technical differences, batch effects, or biological variation. Nonetheless, the data support the conclusion that LCM detected many transcripts missed by scRNA-Seq.

results.result: Gene Ontology analysis revealed that intestine-enriched transcripts are involved in diverse digestive physiology functions including metabolism, transport, vesicular trafficking, organelle physiology, cell shape/motility, and innate immunity. Over 70 solute carrier transporters, nearly 30 Rab GTPases, and over 30 TRAFs were identified. Overlap with transcripts upregulated in response to microbiome dysbiosis or pathogenic bacteria supports a role in innate immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C83 present GO analysis results with specific gene counts and functional categories. Figure 6 and supplementary files provide supporting data. The overlap with immunity-related transcripts from prior studies (C82-C83) strengthens the functional inferences. The analysis is comprehensive and well-supported.

results.result: Cell-type-specific and mediolateral GO analysis suggested that phagocytes perform most general digestive functions, basal cells play roles in metabolism and energy processing, and goblet cells influence extracellular matrix organization and lipid metabolism. Medial transcripts were enriched for innate immunity and macromolecular catabolism, while lateral transcripts were enriched for extracellular matrix organization. Many medially and laterally enriched transcripts were expressed by goblet cells, suggesting functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C90 present cell-type and regional GO analysis. The inferences about cell-type functions (C85-C86, C90) are appropriately qualified as suggestions based on GO enrichment. Figure 6—figure supplement 2 provides supporting data. The conclusions are reasonable given the data, though functional validation would strengthen these claims.

results.result: Goblet cells express genes predicted to regulate luminal digestion (carboxypeptidase A2, lipase F), extracellular matrix remodeling (kallikreins), innate immunity (pgrp-1b), and enteroendocrine-like functions (pcsk1). Surprisingly, gel-forming mucins were expressed by peripharyngeal cells, not goblet cells, suggesting mucin delivery to the intestinal lumen through the pharynx.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C100 describe goblet cell gene expression with functional predictions based on homology and GO analysis. Expression patterns are validated by WISH and FISH (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). The inference about enteroendocrine-like function (C98) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion. The unexpected mucin expression pattern (C99-C100) is clearly documented and represents a potential difference from vertebrate goblet cells.

results.result: Reciprocal best homology searches identified 5,583 planarian transcripts with high homology to human proteins, including 699 intestine-enriched transcripts. The planarian intestine was most similar to human digestive organs (duodenum, small intestine, gallbladder) and liver, with enrichment for genes regulating endodermal specification, bile transport, lipid metabolism, and glucose transport, indicating that physiological roles performed by multiple human organs are consolidated in the planarian intestine.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C101-C107 present comparative analysis with human tissues. The RBH approach is appropriate for identifying orthologs. Figure 7 provides supporting data showing enrichment in digestive tissues. The conclusion about functional consolidation (C107) is a reasonable inference from the data, though it relies on homology-based functional predictions.

results.result: RNAi screening of 22 intestine-enriched transcription factors identified gli-1 and RREB2 as regulators of goblet cells. gli-1 knockdown caused failure of goblet cell regeneration in new intestinal branches, particularly at the midline, while RREB2 knockdown reduced goblet cells in pre-existing tissue, especially lateral branches. Both knockdowns were specific to goblet cells, with phagocytes and basal cells unaffected. The results suggest gli-1 regulates goblet cell differentiation in regenerating tissue, while RREB2 controls maintenance or survival after differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C32, C108-C117 describe RNAi phenotypes with specific spatial and temporal patterns. Figure 8 provides extensive FISH data showing goblet cell loss in different contexts. The specificity of effects (C111, C115) strengthens the conclusions. The inferences about differentiation vs. maintenance roles (C116-C117) are reasonable interpretations of the distinct phenotypes, though mechanistic details remain to be determined.

results.result: In uninjured animals, gli-1 knockdown preferentially reduced lateral goblet cells while medial cells were less affected, whereas RREB2 knockdown reduced both medial and lateral goblet cells, though some lateral cells remained. In regenerates, both knockdowns affected medial and lateral subpopulations similarly. These complex observations suggest mechanisms regulating goblet cell differentiation and maintenance may differ during homeostasis and regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C126 describe differential effects of gli-1 and RREB2 knockdown on medial/lateral goblet cell subpopulations in different contexts. Figure 8—figure supplement 3 provides supporting FISH data. The inference about different mechanisms in homeostasis vs. regeneration (C126) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion and acknowledges alternative explanations (compensatory mechanisms). The data support the complexity of the phenotypes.

results.result: gli-1 and RREB2 mRNAs are not exclusively expressed in goblet cells but are also found in phagocytes, basal cells, and/or intestine-associated muscle. Knockdown of two other basal-enriched transcription factors (PTF1A and lhx2b) also modestly reduced goblet cells, raising the possibility that basal cells (and possibly phagocytes or muscle cells) may non-autonomously influence goblet cell differentiation and/or survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C133 describe expression patterns and phenotypes that complicate interpretation of gli-1 and RREB2 functions. Figure 8—figure supplement 4 shows expression in multiple cell types. The inference about non-autonomous effects (C133) is appropriately qualified as a possibility. The data support the complexity but do not definitively establish cell-autonomous vs. non-autonomous mechanisms.

results.result: Some gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) planarians refused food after 4-5 weeks of dsRNA feeding (1x/week), and some eventually lysed, curled, or died, suggesting goblet cells are required for viability. Feeding failure was only observed with 1x/week feeding, not 2x/week, suggesting goblet cells may regulate hunger or digestive physiology primarily in starved animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C139 describe viability and feeding phenotypes. Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 6 provide supporting data. The inference that goblet cells are required for viability (C136) is reasonable given the lethality, though the text acknowledges alternative explanations (functions in other cell types). The feeding frequency observation (C138-C139) is intriguing and suggests a starvation-related role, consistent with pcsk1 expression.

results.result: In gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cell depletion was robust, but brain, pharynx, other intestinal cell types, and new intestinal branches all regenerated normally, suggesting goblet cells are broadly dispensable for regeneration and their primary role may be to regulate appetite or other aspects of intestinal physiology contributing to viability.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C142 describe regeneration phenotypes showing specificity to goblet cells. Figure 8E shows normal brain and pharynx regeneration. The conclusion that goblet cells are dispensable for regeneration (C141) is well-supported. The inference about their primary role (C142) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion and acknowledges that functions in other cell types could underlie the phenotypes.

results.result: The introduction provides extensive background on digestive tract damage and repair in various organisms, planarian regeneration biology, intestinal morphology and remodeling, intestinal cell types and differentiation, and prior methods for studying planarian intestinal cells, all supported by citations to published literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C28 are background statements supported by citations to published literature. These establish context for the study and are appropriately referenced. No evaluation of the accuracy of cited work is possible without reviewing the original sources, but the claims are presented as established knowledge with proper attribution.

results.result: The manuscript cites prior work stating that kallikreins are expressed by goblet cells in rat, cat, and mouse intestines, and that prohormone convertases function in neurons and endocrine cells in vertebrates and invertebrates to regulate glucose levels, energy homeostasis, and appetite.
results.evaluation: Claims C93 and C97 are statements about prior work supported by citations. These provide context for interpreting the planarian data. The claims are appropriately attributed to published sources.
